text: Indian Citizenship Case Law: Applicant-Focused Precedent Handbook. Birth · Descent · Registration · Naturalisation · Foreign Citizenship · OCI · Delays · Deprivation · Special Frameworks Plain-language legal reference. Verify the current official text, rules, notifications and case status before relying on this guide for an application or legal proceeding. Version: 28 September 2026
headings: Indian Citizenship Case Law: Applicant-Focused Precedent Handbook

text: Contents. - 1 Part I - How to use this case-law handbook - 2 Part II - Standard case-reading template - 3 Part III - Cases on citizenship by birth - 4 Part IV - Cases on citizenship by descent / foreign citizenship - 5 Part V - Cases on registration, residence and naturalisation - 6 Part VI - Cases on OCI - 7 Part VII - Cases on administrative delay, rejection and remedies - 8 Part VIII - Deprivation and citizenship-status disputes - 9 Part IX - CAA / Section 6A / Section 6B litigation - 10 Part X - Master case table and statutory index

Important note. This handbook summarizes selected Indian citizenship judgments and orders for research. A case summary is not the judgment. Always read the original decision before relying on a proposition in litigation or a citizenship application. Case status can change through review, appeal, clarification or later legislation.

Case selection principle. The cases below are organized around applicant problems rather than merely by court or year. The goal is to answer: what was the factual problem, what statutory provision mattered, what did the court decide, and how should an applicant use the decision without overgeneralizing it?

Case 3.1 - Rinzin Dolma & connected matters. Court: Delhi High Court Date: 13 April 2017 Citation / Case No.: W.P.(C) 254/2017 and connected petitions Key provisions: Citizenship Act, Section 3; Passport Act
Facts. The petitioners were born in India at different dates and claimed citizenship under Section 3. The dispute arose when passports were sought and citizenship was questioned.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether persons falling within Section 3 could be treated as Indian citizens for passport purposes. - 2 How the date of birth and the relevant version of Section 3 affected the claim.
Decision / holding. The Court held that the petitioners covered by Section 3 were citizens and directed that passports be issued subject to the ordinary checks and formalities under passport law.

Applicant significance. If your claim is citizenship by birth, the case shows why the exact date of birth and the statutory version applicable to that date are central. It also shows that citizenship status and passport issuance are related but distinct questions.

Limits of the case. The decision concerned the specific petitioners and their statutory facts. It should not be read as saying every person born in India is a citizen irrespective of date or parental status.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/7975822/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/7975822/)

Case 4.1 - Union of India v. Pranav Srinivasan. Court: Supreme Court of India Date: 18 October 2024 Citation / Case No.: 2024 INSC 792; Civil Appeal No. 5932 of 2023 with W.P.(C) No. 123 of 2024 Key provisions: Constitution Articles 8-11; Citizenship Act Sections 5, 8 and 9
headings: Case 4.1 - Union of India v. Pranav Srinivasan

text: Facts. Pranav Srinivasan was born in Singapore in 1999. His parents, born in India, had acquired Singapore citizenship before his birth. He later sought resumption of Indian citizenship under Section 8(2). The Supreme Court considered whether the statutory route permitted resumption and whether other constitutional/statutory routes automatically applied.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether Section 8(2) permitted resumption on the facts. - 2 Whether Article 8 or Section 5(1)(b) independently created the claimed entitlement. - 3 How strictly the statutory eligibility language should be applied.

Decision / holding. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court decisions and held that the claimant had not resumed Indian citizenship under Section 8(2). It emphasized that citizenship cannot be conferred by departing from the plain statutory requirements. The judgment left open the possibility of applying under Section 5(1)(f), subject to its twelve-month ordinary-residence requirement and the Central Government's statutory relaxation power in special circumstances.

Applicant significance. For a person born abroad to parents who later acquired foreign citizenship, this is a major warning against relying only on ancestral connection. Identify the exact statutory route and satisfy its conditions.

Limits of the case. The case is fact-specific. It does not establish a universal rule for every child born abroad; Section 4, the date of birth, parental citizenship at birth, registration requirements and Section 9 issues must be separately examined.

Primary source. [https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2023/21809/21809_2023_6_1502_56499_Judgement_18-Oct-2024.pdf](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2023/21809/21809_2023_6_1502_56499_Judgement_18-Oct-2024.pdf)

Case 4.2 - Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India. Court: Supreme Court of India Date: 16 February 1962 Citation / Case No.: 1962 Supreme Court judgment Key provisions: Constitution Article 9; Citizenship Act Section 9(2); Citizenship Rules evidence provisions
headings: Case 4.2 - Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India

text: Facts. The petitioners challenged provisions dealing with determination of foreign citizenship and the statutory consequences of voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.
Legal issues. - 1 Whether Parliament could provide an evidentiary framework for determining acquisition of foreign citizenship. - 2 Whether Section 9's statutory scheme was constitutionally valid.

Decision / holding. The Supreme Court upheld the relevant framework. Section 9 provides that voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship results in cessation of Indian citizenship, while Section 9(2) provides for determination of questions concerning whether, when or how foreign citizenship was acquired.

Applicant significance. For applicants dealing with dual-nationality or foreign-passport questions, this is a foundational authority showing that the foreign-citizenship question is governed by the Citizenship Act and prescribed evidentiary rules.
Limits of the case. It is an old constitutional decision. Current rules and amendments must still be checked for the precise procedure and evidence.

Primary source. [https://supremecourtindia.in/judgments/supreme-court/1962/izhar-ahmad-khan-vs-union-of-india-1962-02-16/](https://supremecourtindia.in/judgments/supreme-court/1962/izhar-ahmad-khan-vs-union-of-india-1962-02-16/)

Case 4.3 - Reena Chandy v. Union of India. Court: Kerala High Court Date: 7 September 2026 Citation / Case No.: WP(C) No. 28670 of 2024; 2026:KER:67947 Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 4 and Section 9
headings: Case 4.3 - Reena Chandy v. Union of India

text: Facts. The petitioner claimed citizenship by descent based on an Indian father at the time of her birth in 1953. A foreign passport/citizenship issue arose because she had obtained Singapore citizenship while a minor.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether the applicant was a citizen by descent under Section 4. - 2 Whether acquisition of foreign citizenship while a minor could be treated as voluntary acquisition for Section 9 purposes. - 3 Whether the Central Government had applied the correct legal test to the status determination.

Decision / holding. The High Court set aside the challenged determination and directed reconsideration, noting the finding that the petitioner was covered by Section 4 and that acquisition of Singapore citizenship while she was a minor could not simply be treated as her voluntary act.

Applicant significance. This case is useful when the foreign-citizenship event occurred through parents while the claimant was a minor. The factual timeline and proof of how foreign citizenship was acquired become critical.
Limits of the case. It is a High Court decision on the particular record and may be subject to further proceedings. Check current appellate status before relying on it.

Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/docfragment/139703340/?formInput=+indian+citizenship+act+++doctypes%3A+sc%2Chighcourts+year%3A+2026](https://indiankanoon.org/docfragment/139703340/?formInput=+indian+citizenship+act+++doctypes%3A+sc%2Chighcourts+year%3A+2026)
Case 5.1 - Shantanu Prakash v. Union of India. Court: Delhi High Court Date: 30 March 2026 Citation / Case No.: WP(C) 10428/2024 Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 5(1)(a)
headings: Case 5.1 - Shantanu Prakash v. Union of India

text: Facts. The petition challenged rejection of a citizenship application under Section 5(1)(a). The stated reasons included adverse remarks based on FIRs reported by security and police agencies.
Legal issues. - 1 Whether the rejection decision was legally sustainable on the reasons recorded. - 2 How the adverse police/security material affected the citizenship application.

Decision / holding. The order records the challenge to the rejection and the statutory setting. The case is particularly relevant to the interaction between Section 5 applications and adverse police/security material.
Applicant significance. Use this case when the core issue is a rejection based on criminal/security reports. The exact order and subsequent proceedings should be read before drawing a general rule.

Limits of the case. The existence of FIRs does not by itself create a universal statutory bar in every citizenship category; the decision-maker's reasons, the applicable category and the procedural history matter.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168928442/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168928442/)

Case 5.2 - Munna Mohammed Grouse v. Union of India. Court: High Court of Karnataka Date: 22 April 2026 Citation / Case No.: 2026 High Court order Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 5(1)(f); Citizenship Rules
headings: Case 5.2 - Munna Mohammed Grouse v. Union of India

text: Facts. The petition concerned an applicant relying on an earlier Indian-citizen parent and ordinary residence in India. The government argued that the Section 5(1)(f) requirements, the applicable form, undertaking and oath had to be satisfied.
Legal issues. - 1 What statutory conditions applied to the registration claim. - 2 Whether humanitarian/family considerations could replace statutory eligibility.

Decision / holding. The order records the statutory eligibility framework and the government's position that the applicant had to satisfy the prescribed Section 5 route and Rules. It is useful primarily as an example of the court examining the statutory route rather than treating family hardship as an automatic substitute for eligibility.
Applicant significance. Applicants should identify the exact Section 5 clause before relying on family relationships or humanitarian arguments.
Limits of the case. Read the full order and subsequent history before treating it as a definitive precedent on the merits.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/18831002/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/18831002/)

Case 6.1 - Anushka Rengunthwar v. Union of India. Court: Supreme Court of India Date: 3 February 2023 Citation / Case No.: (2023) 11 SCC 209 Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 7B; OCI notification dated 4 March 2021
headings: Case 6.1 - Anushka Rengunthwar v. Union of India

text: Facts. The case concerned OCI cardholders and admission/education-related privileges under the statutory OCI framework.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether OCI holders were entitled to parity with Indian citizens in the relevant educational-admission context. - 2 How Section 7B and the governing notification defined the scope of OCI privileges.

Decision / holding. The Supreme Court treated OCI as a statutory status distinct from citizenship and upheld the policy framework that did not grant OCI holders automatic parity with Indian citizens for the relevant admission issue.

Applicant significance. OCI should be analyzed by the precise statutory right or notification involved. OCI status does not convert into citizenship and does not automatically create every right available to citizens.
Limits of the case. The decision concerns the particular notification and subject matter. Check later OCI notifications for current entitlements.

Primary source. [https://api.sci.gov.in/pdfdate/index1.php?dno=180052021&dt;=2023-02-03&filename;=supremecourt%2F2021%2F18005%2F18005_2021_12_150 1_41507_Judgement_03-Feb-2023.pdf](https://api.sci.gov.in/pdfdate/index1.php?dno=180052021&dt=2023-02-03&filename=supremecourt%2F2021%2F18005%2F18005_2021_12_1501_41507_Judgement_03-Feb-2023.pdf)

Case 6.2 - Khalid Jahangir Qazi through his Power of Attorney v. Union of India. Court: Delhi High Court Date: 11 August 2026 Citation / Case No.: LPA 1239/2024 with connected matters Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 7D; Foreigners Act
headings: Case 6.2 - Khalid Jahangir Qazi through his Power of Attorney v. Union of India

text: Facts. The litigation concerned cancellation of OCI status and subsequent action under the foreigner-control framework. The court considered the distinct statutory position of OCI cardholders and the hearing safeguard in Section 7D.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether an OCI holder remains subject to foreigner law despite OCI privileges. - 2 What procedural protection Section 7D provides before cancellation. - 3 How OCI-specific safeguards interact with separate action under foreigner law.

Decision / holding. The judgment emphasized that OCI cardholders are not Indian citizens and can remain subject to foreigner law. It also addressed the statutory requirement of a reasonable opportunity of hearing before cancellation under Section 7D and the relationship between OCI cancellation and foreigner-law action.

Applicant significance. For an OCI holder facing cancellation or related immigration action, identify each statutory proceeding separately and check whether the applicable procedural safeguards were followed.
Limits of the case. This is a High Court appellate decision and the litigation may continue. Check current appellate status and later orders.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/62109211/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/62109211/)

Case 6.3 - John Robert Roughton III v. Union of India. Court: Delhi High Court Date: 28 March 2025 Citation / Case No.: 2025 High Court decision Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 7B; OCI notification
headings: Case 6.3 - John Robert Roughton III v. Union of India

text: Facts. The case concerned the scope of OCI privileges and the activities for which special permission may be required.
Legal issues. - 1 What privileges are conferred on OCI cardholders. - 2 Whether an OCI holder can rely on the status as if it were Indian citizenship.
Decision / holding. The Court discussed the statutory privilege framework, including multiple-entry lifelong visa and activities requiring special permission under the relevant notification.
Applicant significance. The case is useful for understanding the difference between OCI privileges and unrestricted citizen rights.
Limits of the case. Use the current OCI notification rather than assuming the 2021 list remains unchanged in every detail.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/139609486/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/139609486/)

Case 7.1 - Gurmeet Singh Bains v. Union of India. Court: Punjab & Haryana High Court Date: 30 August 2022 Citation / Case No.: CWP-13636-2022 Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 5(1)(a); Article 226
headings: Case 7.1 - Gurmeet Singh Bains v. Union of India

text: Facts. The petitioner, a Kenyan citizen, had a pending citizenship application. During the delay, the validity of his Kenyan visa/passport became an issue, and he sought directions concerning processing of his citizenship application and related immigration hardship.

Legal issues. - 1 Whether the High Court could intervene in the circumstances of a pending citizenship application. - 2 How delay in citizenship processing interacted with the applicant's foreign passport/visa position.
Decision / holding. The case illustrates the use of Article 226 in a citizenship-processing dispute and the practical consequences that delay can create for a foreign applicant.
Applicant significance. For delayed applicants, preserve evidence of the pending application and explain the concrete legal/practical consequence of delay rather than merely alleging inconvenience.
Limits of the case. The court's powers depend on the specific facts and statutory duties. A writ does not automatically compel grant of citizenship.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168654521/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168654521/)
Case 7.2 - Shantanu Prakash v. Union of India. Court: Delhi High Court Date: 30 March 2026 Citation / Case No.: WP(C) 10428/2024 Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 5(1)(a); Article 226
headings: Case 7.2 - Shantanu Prakash v. Union of India

text: Facts. The applicant challenged a rejection of citizenship based on adverse police/security information.
Legal issues. - 1 Whether the administrative rejection was supported by the recorded reasons. - 2 What role adverse security information played in the decision.

Decision / holding. The order demonstrates a judicial review setting in which the legality of the citizenship authority's rejection is challenged rather than the court simply assuming the role of the original decision-maker.

Applicant significance. Applicants challenging rejection should obtain the actual rejection order, identify the statutory basis, and attack the legally relevant defect rather than merely restating eligibility.
Limits of the case. The cited order should be read in full, including any subsequent order or appeal.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168928442/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/168928442/)

Case 8.1 - Nageshwar Mishra v. Union of India. Court: Allahabad High Court Date: 2 September 2020 Citation / Case No.: 2020 High Court decision Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 10; Constitution Articles 5-11
headings: Case 8.1 - Nageshwar Mishra v. Union of India

text: Facts. The dispute concerned whether the statutory deprivation mechanism under Section 10 could be used against a person whose citizenship arose by birth.
Legal issues. - 1 Who falls within the statutory class that can be deprived under Section 10. - 2 Whether Section 10 could be used merely because a person was born in India.

Decision / holding. The Court emphasized that Section 10 applies to the categories of citizens specified by the statute, including citizens by naturalisation and specified registration/constitutional categories. It rejected treating Section 10 as a general deprivation power over every Indian citizen.
Applicant significance. For citizenship-status disputes, identify the original legal source of citizenship before analyzing Section 10.
Limits of the case. The case is a High Court decision and should be read with the current statutory text and later authority.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/43163736/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/43163736/)
Case 8.2 - Ramesh Singh v. Smt. Sonia Gandhi. Court: Allahabad High Court Date: 11 July 2016 Citation / Case No.: 2016 High Court decision Key provisions: Citizenship Act Sections 5, 9 and 10
headings: Case 8.2 - Ramesh Singh v. Smt. Sonia Gandhi

text: Facts. The litigation involved a challenge to the citizenship status of a person who had been registered as an Indian citizen. The court considered whether it could independently conduct a citizenship inquiry while the registration order remained operative.
Legal issues. - 1 Whether a court could simply disregard an existing citizenship registration order. - 2 What statutory mechanisms existed for termination or deprivation.

Decision / holding. The Court held that, so long as the registration order stood and had not been cancelled/withdrawn or otherwise displaced under the statutory mechanisms, the court could not simply treat the person as not being a citizen on its own.

Applicant significance. Citizenship status should be attacked through the legally prescribed mechanism. An applicant or challenger should identify the operative certificate/order and the statutory route for disputing it.
Limits of the case. The case concerns a specific election-related challenge and should not be generalized beyond the procedural point it addresses.
Primary source. [https://indiankanoon.org/doc/149875120/](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/149875120/)

Case 9.1 - In Re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955. Court: Supreme Court of India Date: 17 October 2024 final decision Citation / Case No.: W.P.(C) No. 274/2009 and connected proceedings Key provisions: Citizenship Act Section 6A; Constitution
headings: Case 9.1 - In Re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955

text: Facts. The litigation challenged the constitutional validity and operation of Section 6A, the Assam Accord-related citizenship framework.
Legal issues. - 1 Whether Section 6A was constitutionally valid. - 2 How the statutory citizenship framework interacted with the Assam Accord and constitutional provisions.

Decision / holding. The Supreme Court's 2024 judgment addressed the constitutional challenge to Section 6A and is a major authority for applicants whose facts fall within the Assam-specific framework.
Applicant significance. Do not apply Section 6A as a generic citizenship route. It is a specialized statutory framework with date-specific migration categories.
Limits of the case. The judgment is constitutionally significant but does not replace the need to examine the applicant's individual date, residence and documentary facts.

Primary source. [https://www.sci.gov.in/hi/%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%95-%E0%A4%85%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%B2%E0% A4%BF%E0%A4%AA%E0%A4%BF-2/](https://www.sci.gov.in/hi/%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%95-%E0%A4%85%E0%A4%A8%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%B2%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AA%E0%A4%BF-2/)

9.2 - Section 6B: current administrative litigation note. Section 6B implementation is more procedure-sensitive than many older citizenship categories because the 2024 Rules and subsequent 2026 changes created specific administrative arrangements. As of August 2026, MHA's current materials show a Collector-centered process for Section 6B applications in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, West Bengal, Assam except tribal areas, Tripura except tribal areas, and the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. This is a current administrative rule/order rather than a court precedent, so it belongs in a case-law handbook as a cross-reference rather than being presented as a judicial holding. [MHA current Acts/Rules page](https://www.mha.gov.in/en/divisionofmha/foreigners-division)

Applicant problem index. Born in India / passport denied, Start with = Rinzin Dolma. Born abroad / Indian parent, Start with = Section 4 + Pranav / Reena Chandy. Foreign citizenship or foreign passport, Start with = Izhar Ahmad Khan + Section 9. Citizenship registration rejected, Start with = Shantanu Prakash / Munna Mohammed Grouse. OCI cancellation, Start with = Khalid Jahangir Qazi. OCI educational privilege, Start with = Anushka Rengunthwar. OCI work/permission issue, Start with = John Robert Roughton III + current OCI notification. Application delayed, Start with = Gurmeet Singh Bains. Deprivation question, Start with = Nageshwar Mishra. Existing citizenship certificate challenged, Start with = Ramesh Singh. Assam Accord citizenship issue, Start with = In Re Section 6A

Source discipline. For current law, prioritize MHA/India Code/Gazette material. For case law, prioritize the Supreme Court or the relevant High Court's official judgment/order portal. Secondary repositories such as Indian Kanoon are useful for discovery and text access but should not replace verification against the original judgment when the case is legally important.

Companion document. Use PDF-1 to determine the legal route and application workflow. Use this PDF-2 to investigate the judicial decisions relevant to the specific problem. The two documents are designed to be read together.
